documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                             )
       Interconnection of Large Loads                        )                Docket No. RM26-4-000
       to the Interstate Transmission System                 )


                            COMMENTS OF ADVANCED ENERGY UNITED

           Advanced Energy United appreciates the opportunity to provide input to the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) in response to the letter from the

Secretary of the Department of Energy (“DOE”) pursuant to Section 403 of the DOE

Organization Act (“DOE Act”) directing FERC to initiate rulemaking procedures regarding the

interconnection of large loads (“Large Loads Letter”).1 The Large Loads Letter contains an

Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“ANOPR”), including fourteen principles for

addressing issues relating to the interconnection of large loads directly to transmission facilities,

and requests that the Commission take final action no later than April 30, 2026.2 Advanced

Energy United is supportive of efforts by DOE and the Commission to expediently resolve

uncertainties and advance efficiencies with respect to the rules governing large load additions.

Our comments below offer recommendations to successfully achieve the objective of the Large

Loads Letter to ensure that “large loads, including AI data centers, served by public utilities must




1
 Letter from Chris Wright, Sec’y of Energy, U.S. Dep’t of Energy, to the Fed. Energy Regul. Comm’n (Oct. 23,
2025) (“Large Loads Letter” or “ANOPR”).
2
    Large Loads Letter, at 2.



                                                                                                               1
 be able to connect to the transmission system in a timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory

manner.”3


     I.    INTRODUCTION

           Load growth is a signal of economic strength, but the pace and scale at which it is

currently projected to materialize is posing a series of well-documented challenges, ranging from

potential resource adequacy shortfalls to concerns that the cost of serving new large loads may

spill over to other customers. Navigating through the current era of load growth in a way that

supports economic growth while also maintaining energy affordability and reliability is the top

challenge facing the entirety of the electricity industry—from private companies to public

utilities to non-profit grid operators to experts and advocates to regulators and elected officials.

DOE’s initiative and leadership in proposing creative and bold solutions and FERC’s quick

response to initiate a rulemaking proceeding and accept stakeholder comments indicate an

understanding of the urgency and importance of the task at hand, and signal an encouraging

commitment to meaningful reform.

           The solutions to the challenges that rapid load growth poses are at once simple and

complex. At the core, accommodating load growth is a question of investing in infrastructure:

generation and storage resources, transmission and distribution upgrades, advanced grid

management, and customer-sited technologies for resilience and flexibility. Delivering these

solutions involves integrated system planning and clear and fair market rules to ensure an

efficient and reliable resource mix. The Commission has already taken important actions through

rulemakings like Order Nos. 2222, 2023, and 1920 and 1920-A that will, when fully



3
    Large Loads Letter at 1.



                                                                                                       2
 implemented, better equip grid operators, transmission providers, and market participants to

prepare for load growth and any other future challenges. But there is a lag between issuance of

reforms and full implementation, and additional delay before the resulting physical infrastructure

reaches commercial operation and is able to generate, store, avoid, shift, and/or transmit

electrons to serve new load.

           While the medium- to long-term solutions to meeting load growth are already underway,

new large loads can often materialize much more quickly than the infrastructure to serve them. If

we try to force too much new load onto an unprepared grid, the result will be reliability shortfalls

and price spikes that adversely impact all customers. And if we build new infrastructure to meet

forecasts that turn out to have been inflated, reliability concerns may be minimized, but the cost

impacts to all customers will be exacerbated. At the same time, new large loads are presenting

novel challenges due to their scale and operating characteristics. The question at the heart of this

proceeding is how to enable speed to power for new large loads in a way that is transparent,

durable, fair for all customers, and consistent with the requirements of the Federal Power Act

(“FPA”) to avoid undue discrimination and ensure just and reasonable rates.

           The ANOPR rightly emphasizes the long-standing principle of open access transmission

service, citing improvements to transmission planning and generator interconnection that have

stemmed from and served to bolster this foundational principle.4 The load interconnection

process today is characterized by long delays and lack of transparency 5—not the hallmarks of a

5
  See Google comments to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., RE: Critical Issue Fast Path – Large Load Additions,
available at https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-lla/postings/20250828-stakeholder-
comments-cifp-lla.pdf, at 5 (“Existing large load interconnection processes, especially in areas with a significant
volume of requests, have become overwhelmed and insufficient, and interconnecting customers are facing
interconnection times of several years, at best, and unknown times at worst, with little insight into the constraints
driving those timelines or how interconnection requests are differentiated among customers.”)



                                                                                                                        3
 system in which open and non-discriminatory access to the transmission system is assured. Many

states and regions are already stepping in to rectify a clearly broken process, ranging from PJM’s

Large Load Additions Critical Issue Fast Path (CIFP) process 6 to SPP’s efforts to accommodate

large loads through various High Impact Large Load pathways7 to a growing number of state-

jurisdictional large load tariffs. 8 The interrelated task of improving load forecasting has also

rightly received increased attention, as the (in)accuracy of our load forecasts will determine

whether our responses to impending load growth are appropriately tailored to the scale and scope

of the challenge.9

        The Commission can and must play a role in providing clarity to the large load

interconnection process and to the various rules and processes that impact and are impacted by

large load additions. Given its national purview and broad authority, the Commission is uniquely

positioned to gather information from across these efforts and from all involved stakeholders to

identify the areas where Commission involvement is necessary to ensure open access to the

transmission system, where it will prove beneficial in accelerating and clarifying progress, and

where it may conversely impede or complicate efficient implementation of solutions. As the



6
 Letter from David E. Mills, PJM Board of Managers Chair, PJM, Interconnection, L.L.C. to PJM Stakeholders
(Aug. 8, 2025). https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2025/20250808-
pjm-board-letter-re-implementation-of-critical-issue-fast-path-process-for-large-load-additions.pdf
7
 Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Tariff Revisions to Add the High Impact Large Load Processes and High Impact
Large Load Generation Assessment, Submitted in Docket No. ER26-247, (October 24, 2025) (“HILL/HILLGA
Filing”).
8

West Virginia service territory, and in American Electric Power’s (“AEP”) Ohio service territory. Virginia Electric
and Power Company (“Dominion”) and APCo Virginia have large load tariff provisions pending before the Virginia
State Corporation Commission; final outcomes are expected by the end of 2025. Additionally, Commonwealth
Edison (“ComEd”) has proposed large load tariff revisions.
9
 Advanced Energy United, Pre-Technical Conference Comments, Docket No. AD25-7-000, at 2 (May 16, 2025);
Letter from Chairman Rosner, Federal Energy Regul. Comm’n, to Reg’l Transmission Operators and Indep. Sys.
Operators (Sept. 18, 2025); Letter from Electricity Customer Alliance, to Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
(May 30, 2025).



                                                                                                                  4
 Commission approaches the complex and exciting challenges laid out in the Large Loads Letter

and accompanying ANOPR, Advanced Energy United urges an approach that is:

   •   Affordable. Consistent with the requirement of the FPA to ensure just and reasonable
       rates, any rules regarding large load interconnections must promote affordability for all
       customers.

   •   Reliable. Ensuring safe and reliable electricity is at the core of the Commission’s
       mission, and rules governing large load additions should ensure that reliability is not
       compromised by the influx of new large loads. The Commission should work closely
       with the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) to achieve this
       objective.

   •   Fair. Consistent with the FPA, the Commission must protect against undue
       discrimination and ensure just and reasonable rates by avoiding adverse impacts on other
       market participants and other (non-large load) customers. This means avoiding any
       adverse impacts to reliability and resource adequacy, avoiding undue preference to large
       loads and/or the resources serving them, not interfering with clear and fair market signals
       and rules for all market participants, and ensuring that cost causers bear appropriate costs
       by protecting against direct or indirect cost shifts.

   •   Efficient. Any actions taken by the Commission should support the goal of speed to
       power, and should avoid disrupting progress as reforms are debated and implemented. In
       some areas, Commission intervention may provide necessary standardization and
       transparency that promotes efficiency, while in other areas it may add risk of delay or
       complexity. The record in this proceeding will be instructive in identifying reforms to
       prioritize and those to avoid or approach with more caution.

   •   Durable. While this proceeding is a response to the acute challenge of rapid data center
       load growth, the solutions it produces should avoid disrupting long-term market and
       business certainty, good long-term planning practices, and fair and open access to the
       transmission system, consistent with all applicable statutes and legal precedent. To the
       extent temporary measures are considered, they should be designed such that they
       support, rather than conflict with, long-term solutions.


Advanced Energy United’s comments below are offered with these overarching goals in mind,

and we look forward to continuing to work with the Commission, DOE, the RTOs/ISOs, states,

and other stakeholders to enact solutions that enable speed to power without eroding critical

guardrails that have and will continue to serve all customers well.


 II.   COMMENTS


                                                                                                   5
                A. Jurisdiction

           United agrees with DOE that FERC has an important role to play in providing clarity and

addressing the challenges of large load additions. As DOE explains in the ANOPR, section

201(b) of the Federal Power Act (FPA) grants the Commission jurisdiction over the sale of

wholesale electricity in interstate commerce and over the transmission of electricity in interstate

commerce.10 This commonly accepted basis for the Commission’s jurisdiction clearly grants the

Commission an important role in the interconnection of new large loads to the transmission

system. At minimum, this makes the Commission responsible for clarifying treatment of

different large load and co-location arrangements with respect to their impact on and use of

wholesale services and the interstate transmission system; ensuring that load forecasts used in

FERC-jurisdictional planning processes and impacting FERC-jurisdictional markets are accurate;

ensuring open access to the transmission system; maintaining just and reasonable rates; and

ensuring reliability as large loads come online.

           It is important that FERC make clear that regardless of the role FERC plays in large load

interconnection arrangements, states retain jurisdiction over retail sales to large loads. As noted

in United’s response to the PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 206 Investigation, states and the

Commission share a service responsibility to co-located load and generation. 11 Importantly,

many states are already taking steps to address challenges and implement solutions related to

large loads. For example, in February 2025, Indiana passed tariff revisions to set terms for new




10
     16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1).
11
  Response of Advanced Energy United to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s Answer to the Show Cause Order, EL25-
49-000, at 8 (April 23, 2025).



                                                                                                          6
 large load connections requiring that new large loads pay for grid upgrades needed to connect. 12

Similarly, Texas and Nevada have also made tariff revisions to account for large load

interconnection upgrades.13 Acting according to their historical jurisdiction over all load

interconnections, states have made efforts to control the rapid growth of demand due to the

influx of large load interconnection requests. While the scope of the ANOPR extends beyond

these state-level efforts, there is overlap and consistency with some of the principles of the

ANOPR, and these state efforts should be taken into account as the Commission contemplates a

potential rulemaking.

         While the substance of United’s comments below apply to the topic of large load

interconnection regardless of jurisdiction, some elements of the proposed changes could be

undertaken by the Commission under a status quo exercise of its jurisdiction with respect to large

load interconnection. United encourages the Commission, in any future proposal, to make clear

which elements of the proposed reforms are not contingent upon the assertion that the

Commission has broader jurisdiction over large loads interconnecting to the transmission system,

and consider advancing these on an accelerated basis. These reforms may include, but not be

limited to:

     •   Requiring that transmission providers study large loads and interconnecting supply

         resources concurrently, with appropriate guardrails as discussed below (Principle Three);

https://www.utilitydive.com/news/indiana-iurc-large-load-interconnection-data-center-aep-amazon-google/740452/.
13
  Arcelia Martin, Texas Grid Operators and Regulators Iron Out New Rules for Data Centers, Inside Climate News
(Oct. 10, 2025), https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10102025/texas-grid-operators-and-regulators-iron-out-new-
rules-for-data-centers/. Elaine Goodman, Large-Load Tariffs Touted as Alternative to ‘Side Deals’, RTO Insider
(Sept. 4, 2025), https://www.rtoinsider.com/114017-nm-regulators-study-large-load-rate-design/.



                                                                                                              7
     •   Requiring stricter standards for load forecasting for the purposes of transmission planning

        and as an input into resource adequacy constructs (related to Principle Four);

    •   Clarifying how different configurations of hybrid / co-located load plus generation

        resources would be studied, and how the cost of network transmission charges, ancillary

        services, and other wholesale costs would be assessed (Principles Five, Eleven, and

        Twelve);

    •   Taking steps to encourage and expand flexibility for large loads and non-large loads alike

        (Principle Seven); and

    •   Requiring that any existing facilities that seek to enter partial suspension to serve a new

        load at the same location must go through a system support resource or reliability must

        run (RMR) type study, and that such studies should include evaluation of potential

        resource adequacy concerns (Principle Ten).

Where relevant, the comments below call out opportunities for the Commission to take action

without asserting exclusive jurisdiction over large loads interconnecting directly to transmission

facilities.


              B. Proposed Principles for Large Load Interconnection

        Advanced Energy United provides the following comments in response to the fourteen

principles laid out by DOE, listed in the order they appear in the ANOPR. Following DOE’s

proposed principles, United offers some additional considerations and principles for the

Commission’s consideration.


                      1. Principles One and Two: If FERC moves forward with asserting
                         jurisdiction over large loads interconnecting to transmission
                         facilities, it must clearly define upfront when the Commission-
                         jurisdictional process would apply.


                                                                                                      8
           The ANOPR proposes as its first principle that FERC jurisdiction be “limited to

interconnections directly to transmission facilities, consistent with the Commission's seven-

factor test.”14 The ANOPR likewise acknowledges that states preserve jurisdiction over

generation facilities, facilities used in local distribution or only for transmission of electricity in

intrastate commerce, and transmission consumed by the transmitter. The ANOPR further

proposes as principle two that the “the reforms should only apply to new loads greater than 20

MW and, for hybrid facilities, where the load is greater than 20 MW.” 15 The ANOPR requests

comment on the specific 20 MW threshold, as well as whether a threshold is necessary at all.

          Should FERC assert its jurisdiction over large load interconnection, it must clearly limit

its jurisdiction to large loads connecting to transmission facilities as suggested in the ANOPR.

However, reliance on the “seven factor test” alone is insufficient to avoid potential uncertainty at

the boundary of state and federal jurisdiction, which could cause unnecessary delay and added

cost to the large load interconnection process, contrary to DOE’s stated goal of achieving speed

to power. To avoid such an outcome, there must be clear definitions for what constitutes

“transmission facilities” and what constitutes “large load” for purposes of FERC-jurisdictional

large load interconnection.

          With respect to “transmission facilities,” as acknowledged above, should FERC choose to

assert its jurisdiction over large load interconnection, such jurisdiction must be strictly limited to

those loads interconnecting directly to interstate transmission. To avoid overriding state authority

and to avoid costly and time-consuming confusion, the Commission should provide upfront

clarity regarding whether the FERC-jurisdictional process applies to a particular interconnection


14
     ANOPR at P 18.
15
     ANOPR at P 19.



                                                                                                          9
 request to ensure that all large load interconnection customers know which process applies.

Failure to provide this upfront clarity will add an otherwise unnecessary step of identifying

which process applies to a particular interconnection request, which may introduce delay and

confusion and even unnecessary litigation during the interconnection process. The Commission

has previously recognized the potential for lack of certainty regarding jurisdictional boundaries

and the adverse impact it can have on the generator interconnection process; this effect would be

equally the case for large load interconnections. For example, in 2022, the Commission accepted

a filing from ISO-New England (ISO-NE) to resolve inefficiencies with Distributed Energy

Resources (DERs) connecting to the grid due to conflicting understandings of whether the ISO-

NE or state interconnection process applied. 16 This confusion arose because transmission

operators did not have a clear map of which feeders were FERC-jurisdictional versus state-

jurisdictional.17 Some interconnection customers discovered very late in the process that they had

been following the wrong process, through no fault of their own, adding significant delays and

unnecessary costs and regulatory processes. When applied to multi-billion dollar investment in

infrastructure to serve a large load like a data center, such confusion and delay would be

catastrophic.

           United suggests that one potential approach to clarifying when a FERC-jurisdictional

large load jurisdiction process should apply is to establish a rebuttable presumption that any large

load interconnection above a certain voltage threshold is defined as interconnecting to a

“transmission facility” subject to FERC jurisdiction for purposes of large load interconnections.

A voltage threshold would clearly define when the FERC process applies, avoiding confusion



16
     ER22-2226-000, Letter for Interconnection Jurisdiction Tariff Revisions, ISO-NE (June 29, 2022).
17
     180 FERC ¶ 61, 129, at P 19 (Aug 26, 2022).



                                                                                                        10
 and potential discrimination. There are already RTO proposals to create such a threshold

definition to clearly delineate when more stringent study processes should apply: the pending

SPP High Impact Large Load Integration proposal sets forth such a threshold to clarify where

additional load interconnection requirements apply.18

           Setting a voltage threshold may also obviate the need for a MW threshold below which

the FERC process does not apply. However, should the Commission adopt such a threshold,

United notes that the 20 MW threshold put forward in the ANOPR is significantly lower than the

definition of “large load” already in use in states that have taken action to standardize large load

interconnections. For example, Texas statute defines large load as any load above 75 MW,19 and

the recent Indiana & Michigan power settlement defined large load customer as a customer with

contract capacity greater than or equal to 70 MW at an individual plant.20 The Commission

should also clarify that existing loads that expand incrementally, e.g., due to electrification of

certain industrial processes, should not trigger an entire FERC-jurisdictional re-study if the

incremental load increase causes the facility’s load to exceed the MW threshold used to define

large loads. At the same time, the Commission must avoid a structure that would enable new

large loads to evade FERC jurisdiction by connecting initially just below the threshold, and

adding incremental load after interconnecting. Reliance on a voltage threshold alone would avoid

such circumstances while still functionally limiting FERC’s jurisdiction to large loads.

                        2. Principle Three: Studying load or hybrid facilities jointly with
                          generating facilities is a logical approach, but clear guardrails are
                          necessary to avoid undue discrimination and ensure just and
                          reasonable rates.

          The ANOPR proposes that “to the extent practicable, load and hybrid facilities should be

studied together with generating facilities,” and explains that “siting a large load near or at the

same point of interconnection as a new generating facility could reduce the network upgrades

needed to interconnect only the load or only the generating facility.” 21 United agrees with this

rationale, but cautions that this principle must be narrowly tailored to avoid adverse impacts on

both existing load and other interconnection customers. United also notes that the Commission

can enact a version of this principle without shifting how FERC’s jurisdiction is interpreted with

respect to large load interconnection; indeed, SPP has already made a proposal for expedited

study of new generation to serve large loads. 22

          The concept of studying large loads together with supply resources has both near-term,

practical appeal and durable, logical appeal. On a practical level, some regions are already facing

supply shortages such that the only viable pathway to accommodate load growth without

adversely impacting existing customers may be for new large loads to participate in some form

of “Bring Your Own Generation” option. In particular, PJM is undergoing a fast-track

stakeholder process to address Large Load Additions due to projected peak load growth of 32

GW from 2024-2030.23 Bringing online new generation requires a pathway to interconnect the

new generation, which a new load/generation interconnection study process would provide.


21
     ANOPR at P 20.
22
  ER26-247-000, Submission of Tariff Revisions to Add the High Impact Large Load Process and High Impact
Large Load Generation Assessment, Southwest Power Pool.
23
  Letter from David E. Mills, PJM Board of Managers Chair, PJM, Interconnection, L.L.C. to PJM Stakeholders
(Aug. 8, 2025). https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2025/20250808-
pjm-board-letter-re-implementation-of-critical-issue-fast-path-process-for-large-load-additions.pdf



                                                                                                           12
 Beyond this period of acute need for new supply, the idea of studying new large load together

with an associated new generating or storage facility has clear merit for the reasons summarized

in the ANOPR. To the extent that a new large load and new generation or storage resource are

geographically and electrically proximate, studying them together would reduce network

upgrades, lower costs, and reduce the need for critical supply chain components. Establishing a

combined study pathway would incentivize this kind of siting efficiency. Furthermore, the

Commission should clarify that large loads that enter into arrangements with any new and

deliverable capacity resource(s) that are appropriately sited should also be studied together. In

other words, a hybrid facility should not be limited to a large load and a generator, it should also

include a large load and any portfolio of capacity resources—whether generation, battery

storage, demand response, distributed energy resource aggregations, or other accredited resource

types.

         However, a loosely defined load/supply resource interconnection pathway that provides

an expedited pathway for generation interconnection without appropriate safeguards would result

in undue discrimination and unjust and unreasonable rates. Any study pathway that would give

generation or storage facilities a faster, likely lower-cost interconnection pathway relative to the

standard large generator interconnection process (“LGIP”) queue confers advantage to

generating facilities that proceed through this path. To avoid undue discrimination, this pathway

must be designed such that it is specific to the circumstance of a new supply resource being

brought to the system specifically to serve the new large load that justifies its expedited

interconnection. This means (1) this expedited pathway should not confer the same

interconnection service as is available to interconnection customers serving native load, and (2)

this pathway should be available only to generation or storage resources that are not similarly




                                                                                                    13
 situated to other interconnection customers in that they meet eligibility parameters that

meaningfully, transparently, and objectively differentiate projects that proceed via expedited

pathways from projects in the general queue. Requiring merely a contractual link between the

load and generation or a loose geographic link would be unduly discriminatory and would fail to

protect other interconnection customers.

            SPP’s High Impact Large Load Generation Addition (“HILLGA”) proposal currently

pending in Docket No. ER 26-247-00024 is a good starting point for the Commission to adapt in

that it:

       •    Does not provide full interconnection service akin to Network Resource Interconnection

            Service (“NRIS”) or Energy Resource Interconnection Service (“ERIS”), but rather a

            more limited, provisional interconnection allowing the generation to serve the new large

            load (which SPP terms “Load Limited Resource Interconnection Service” or “LLRIS”);25

       •    Limits LLRIS to 5 years and requires the HILLGA to be on a path toward receiving

            transmission service, either firm Long-Term Point-to-Point Transmission Service

            obtained via the Aggregate Transmission Service Study or NRIS/ERIS obtained via the

            standard interconnection process;26 and

       •    Requires meaningful electrical proximity between the load/hybrid facility and the

            generator, defined as no more than two substations away (one if connecting at 765 kV),

            such that the pairing would minimize network upgrades and study complexity and avoid




24
  Southwest Power Pool, Submission of Tariff Revisions to Add the High Impact Large Load
Processes and High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment, Docket No.ER 26-247-000.
25
     Id., at 29.
26
     Id., at 29, 37.



                                                                                                     14
             causing congestion.27 United recognizes that what constitutes “electrical proximity” may

            vary by region; this term should be generally defined to allow consideration of capacity

            deliverable to the associated load such that it relieves, avoids, or minimizes congestion

            impacts.

SPP explicitly designed the HILLGA process with these protections in place to avoid adversely

impacting the standard generator interconnection queue.28 SPP’s filing states that “a customer

cannot use the HILLGA process to bypass” the normal interconnection procedures” and that it

“recognizes the importance of SPP’s standard generator interconnection process and balances use

of that process with a need to interconnect HILLS in an expedited manner on a limited basis

during a short time period.”29 This balance should guide the Commission’s development of

procedures to allow concurrent study of large loads and supply resources.

            While recent improvements to the interconnection process as a result of Order No. 2023

and other reforms will increase the efficiency of the standard generator interconnection process,

it can reasonably be expected that a serial process operating in parallel to study individual supply

resources to serve new large loads will be faster and likely cheaper.30 In the absence of

protections to ensure that such a path is limited and targeted, non-large load customers will be

harmed because interconnection customers proceeding through standard generator

interconnection process to serve all other load customers (primarily existing load) will likely face

a costlier, lengthier path to connect to the grid. This would result in undue discrimination

     Id. at 26.
28
     Id. at 35-38.
29
     Id., at 36.
30
  For example, SPP anticipates that the HILLGA process will be completed in 150 days, compared to 12 months
under its current Definitive Interconnection System Impact Study (DISIS) process. Id., at 36-37.



                                                                                                              15
 amongst similarly situated interconnection customers and would create incentives for

interconnection customers to seek opportunities to serve new large loads rather than serving

native load customers. New large loads would thus gain priority access to the best available

supply resources, regardless of their geographic proximity and other factors. While an expansive

shortcut may be a tempting solution to address near-term load growth needs, it must not be

allowed to undermine the long-term benefits of maintaining a fair and predictable

interconnection process to serve all load. With appropriate guardrails, we can have both: a

streamlined load/supply interconnection process that applies in limited, specific circumstances

that serves to incentivize efficient siting of new large loads and generation, and a fair and

efficient generator interconnection process to serve the majority of interconnection customers

consistent with the mandate to avoid undue discrimination and ensure just and reasonable rates.


                      3. Principle Four: Load and hybrid facilities should be subject to
                         standardized, transparent, and stringent requirements to discipline
                         interconnection requests and enhance load forecasting.

          Drawing from the example of the generator interconnection process, the ANOPR

proposes that “load and hybrid facilities should be subject to standardized study deposits,

readiness requirements, and withdrawal penalties.”31 United directionally supports the concept of

standardizing and increasing the stringency of the load interconnection process, regardless of

whether this process is FERC or state jurisdictional. Should the large load interconnection

process remain state-jurisdictional, United notes that the Commission can still apply this

principle to the load forecasting process at the RTOs to discipline the degree of load growth that

markets and planning processes should be preparing for; in light of the level of anticipated load



31
     ANOPR at P 21.



                                                                                                  16
 growth and the degree of uncertainty regarding that growth, doing so is critical to preserve just

and reasonable rates.

           The ANOPR correctly notes that heightened financial commitments in the form of

deposits and penalties would “deter speculative projects and provide transmission providers with

more useful information to more accurately forecast demand on their systems.” 32 Increasing the

requirements on interconnecting large load customers is critical to ensure that utilities and system

operators are not planning and preparing for load that will not ultimately show up, and that load

is committing to pay the cost of preparing the system. Without this discipline, other new large

loads will suffer the consequences of an interconnection process bogged down by speculative

projects, and all ratepayers risk being left paying the cost of preparing the system for new load

that never materializes.

           The Commission approved, and United supported, a similar approach for generator

interconnection, and the parallel that DOE draws to that process is entirely appropriate. As with

the generator interconnection process, it is critical to ensure compatibility with commercial

realities and to adopt a mix of financial and non-financial readiness requirements to

accommodate a range of business models and avoid a “pay to play” model whereby well-

capitalized large loads may be able to buy their way into multiple queue positions. The Clean

Energy Buyers Association offered several non-financial readiness indicators in AD24-11-000

that the Commission should consider here, including: “(i) Site control documentation, such as

land acquisition or lease agreements; (ii) Permitting progress, with permits approved or in

progress; (iii) Community engagement efforts, demonstrating local support or alignment with




32

                       6. Principle Seven: The Commission should encourage the benefits of
                          load flexibility through expedited interconnection and other means.

           The ANOPR proposes that “the interconnection study of large loads that agree to be

curtailable and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable should be

 expedited.”40 United agrees with the underlying logic that curtailment and/or dispatch of load

and hybrid facilities supports “the timely and orderly addition of large loads to the transmission

system in a safe, reliable, and non-discriminatory manner.”41 However, this principle applies

more broadly, and should be expanded to realize the full benefits of load flexibility to

accommodate rapid growth of new large loads. United supports the ANOPR proposal that load

flexibility should confer the benefit of expedited interconnection, and offers the following

clarifications and recommendations.

           First, this treatment should apply to large loads that agree to be curtailable and

dispatchable or that enter into arrangements with deliverable capacity from flexible loads. Even

a small degree of flexibility among new large loads would enable the current system to

accommodate significantly more load growth with minimal infrastructure upgrades. 42 New large

loads willing to operate without firm transmission access—either permanently on a temporary

basis as network upgrades are planned and constructed—should have clearly defined, optional,

and expedited pathways to do so. At the same time, the role of flexibility as a tool to

accommodate new large loads extends across the entire system: roughly 1–2% of hours each year

(around 100–200 hours) usually account for 15–20% of total peak demand. Thus, deploying

solutions that solve this “200-hour problem” by reducing peak demand during those critical 100-

200 hours can unlock significant grid capacity to accommodate load growth. Such solutions need

not originate at the site of a new large load but could be incremental flexibility that is contracted

by that large load and that is located such that it counteracts the impacts of the new large load.

          The rapid emergence of large loads has created numerous concerns over resource

adequacy and reliability needs, which any regulation or action by the Commission should

address. To the extent an existing generating facility seeks to enter partial or full suspension to

serve an individual customer, it is critical to ensure that network load does not suffer any adverse

consequences, including degradation of reliability or increased costs. The Commission should

require a robust process, including a screen for reliability and stability impacts as well as

resource adequacy impact, to ensure a resource needed for resource adequacy does not pull its

supply from the region to serve an individual customer. The resource adequacy evaluation should

also consider locational impacts; for example, allowing an existing resource to be partially

dedicated to serve a new load within a congested area may not undermine resource adequacy,

even if the broader RTO region is in a reserve deficiency. There are also opportunities to mitigate

the impact of existing generation serving a new large load: Texas recently adopted a requirement

that existing generation undergo a study akin to that contemplated by the ANOPR prior to

serving a new large load through a “net metering” arrangement, while also requiring the capacity

from the “exiting” resource to be available to ERCOT during emergencies.48

         Multiple regions are citing potential resource adequacy shortfalls resulting from rapid

entry of new large loads; it is critical that in solving this problem, we do not create a new one by

pulling needed resources away from existing customers to serve new large loads. Transparent,

well-defined, robust study processes are critical to ensure continued reliability and affordability
